title: Operating Scorecard and Management Follow-Through

epigraph.quote: Q3 was an exceptionally strong quarter across all parts of our business. We now hold 848,517 Bitcoin and recorded a record $21 billion fair value gain on our Bitcoin holdings in Q3.
epigraph.author: Andrew Kang, Chief Financial Officer, Q3 2026 call

web_blocks.html: The statement combines treasury execution and a non-cash valuation result; compare it with software-specific metrics rather than treating the consolidated quarter as one operating outcome. [4]

web_blocks.title: Six KPIs that keep the operating record visible

web_blocks.html: The scorecard below uses only reported software and customer-operating evidence. A useful KPI is not simply a number the company can publish; it should help you distinguish product demand, migration, profitability, and cash generation. Several of the measures below are snapshots because the permitted sources do not provide a full cohort history. Derived percentages are identified as calculations, and the customer outcome measures are company-reported case-study claims rather than audited company-wide operating KPIs. [1][2][3][6][7][8][9]

rows: 1. Total software revenue
Annual revenue was modestly higher; quarterly revenue was lower year over year.
One segment only; no customer cohorts or bookings data. [1][2]
2. Cloud subscription revenue
Subscription revenue expanded in both supplied comparisons.
No renewal, net retention, contract-value, or cohort margin data. [1][2]
3. Revenue-mix transition
FY2025 licenses $39.674m and support $204.225m; Q3 2026 licenses $3.829m and support $37.681m, both below Q3 2025
Cloud growth is occurring alongside lower legacy-related categories in the quarterly comparison.
Nine-month 2026 revenue by individual stream is not in the supplied summary; conversion counts are unavailable. [1][2]
4. Gross profit and margin
FY2025 gross profit $327.816m on $477.233m revenue; Q3 2026 $89.634m on $125.427m, a derived 71.5% margin
Gross profit remains substantial relative to revenue; the release rounds Q3 margin to 71%.
Gross profit does not cover all selling, R&D, and G&A expense in FY2025. [1][2][3]
5. Operating cash flow less capex
FY2025 CFO -$67.241m and capex $8.212m; 9M 2026 CFO $14.267m and capex $3.181m
The nine-month comparison improved, while FY2025 was cash-consuming.
Interim data do not prove a durable full-year trend; detailed working-capital causes are not supplied. [1][2]
6. Customer adoption and outcome evidence
Pfizer reports utilization moving from 10% to 90%; Helsana reports redundancy down '90% plus'; Lotte reports four-times usage and 90% efficiency improvement
Named cases show the kinds of workflow outcomes the platform is intended to support.
All are company-reported examples; no aggregate utilization, retention, or independently verified outcomes. [6][7][9]
web_blocks.note: Revenue, profit, and cash values are reported dollars; derived margin is gross profit divided by revenue. KPI 6 is customer-case evidence, not a company-wide audited KPI. [1][2][6][7][9]

web_blocks.html: These indicators work best as a linked set rather than as six isolated scores. Revenue growth can conceal a mix shift; subscription growth can coincide with loss of support revenue; gross margin can look healthy while sales and administration absorb the remainder; and accounting profit can diverge from cash. The sequence you want is customer adoption, renewal and expansion, recognized recurring revenue, gross profit after delivery costs, and finally cash collected after operating needs. The permitted materials show pieces of that chain—revenue, gross profit, cash flow, and selected customer outcomes—but not the cohort links between them. That is why the scorecard should preserve gaps rather than fill them with proxies. [1][2][5][6][7][8][9]

web_blocks.title: Management’s walk-the-talk record: alignments and open tests

web_blocks.html: The most measurable operating commitment in the permitted transcript concerns the treasury program, not the software roadmap. CEO Phong Le said, “The goal is to double Bitcoin per share in seven years through the use of digital credit.” The Q3 release reports 848,517 Bitcoin held as of October 25, 2026, 26% year-to-date growth, and $14.33 billion of year-to-date purchases. Those are reported execution facts that show the treasury program remained active. They do not yet establish progress toward doubling Bitcoin per share: the seven-year horizon is only beginning, the permitted evidence does not provide a comparable per-share baseline and full issuance schedule, and an asset count is not the same metric as an asset count per share. [3][4]

For software, the observable alignment is directional rather than conclusive. Subscription revenue grew from FY2024 to FY2025 and again in the Q3 year-over-year comparison, consistent with management’s cloud-oriented route to market. At the same time, total Q3 revenue and gross profit were lower year over year, product support and licenses were lower, and full on-premises support is scheduled to end December 31, 2026. The evidence supports “cloud subscriptions are expanding while legacy categories face transition,” not “the transition is complete” or “all lost legacy dollars have been replaced.” No historic dated software commitments, migration targets, or customer-retention targets are supplied for a fuller audit. [1][2]

Kang’s description of Q3 as strong across all parts of the business should be read in context. The company reported Q3 software revenue of $125.427 million versus $128.691 million a year earlier and software gross profit of $89.634 million versus $90.678 million. The release reports a $20.91 billion digital-asset fair-value gain and $19.53 billion net income, while the transcript quote itself highlights a record $21 billion fair-value gain. The software business may have had positive operational developments not captured in those totals, but the aggregate earnings figure is overwhelmingly shaped by asset remeasurement. You need the stream-level and cash measures to test the software claim. [2][3][4]

web_blocks.title: Leadership change is a governance promise to observe

web_blocks.html: The Q3 release said Andrew Kang would leave the CFO role effective November 5, 2026, that CEO Phong Le would cover finance in the interim, and that Reza Virasteh was appointed CFO effective January 2027 as roles were split across software and Bitcoin operations. Le described the planned split on the call: “Starting in January 2027, we will split the CFO role between our software and our Bitcoin businesses, which are quite different.” This structure recognizes distinct operating and financing demands. At the evidence cutoff represented by the Q3 release, the change is an announced transition; the permitted source excerpts do not report its subsequent implementation or whether the new responsibilities improve segment transparency. [3][4]

The release also reports $1.48 billion in cumulative preferred dividends paid, $5.07 billion in USD assets, and 3.4 years of dividend-plus-interest coverage as of October 25. Those are management-reported treasury liquidity facts, not software KPIs. They merit reconciliation against the underlying instruments, obligations, and future cash demands in a later financing review. For this price-blind operational pass, they illustrate why the company’s capital structure needs a separate scorecard from customer demand and software cash conversion. [3]

A complete governance scorecard would also name thresholds in advance. For example, management could report a target for cloud migrations, renewal rates, operating cash generation, or service reliability and then show actual delivery against it. None of those dated software targets appears in the permitted excerpts. You therefore cannot grade the company as having met or missed targets that have not been disclosed here. What you can do is set the baseline: subscription revenue is rising, support and license revenue have weakened in the quarterly comparison, the full-support deadline is fixed, and software cash sufficiency remains a stated concern. [1][2]

web_blocks.title: What should be added to the next operating review

web_blocks.html: To judge follow-through rigorously, you would want quarterly subscription retention and expansion, on-premises-to-cloud migration counts, customer additions and losses, implementation time, product uptime, usage by role, support costs, gross margin by stream, and customer concentration. You would also want the company to distinguish customer-success activity from booked support revenue and explain whether cloud growth is net new, migrated, or expanded spend. Those measures would turn the present directional scorecard into a test of operating promises. Their absence does not prove failure; it limits what can be claimed. [1][2][5]

web_blocks.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
paragraphs: The management record is mixed in a precise way: cloud revenue and treasury purchases show reported follow-through, while cash sufficiency, customer retention, the per-share treasury objective, and the CFO redesign remain unproven in the permitted time series. Separate observable delivery from a target that has not yet had time to mature. [1][2][3][4]

book_paragraphs: You need a scorecard that separates the customer operation from the treasury operation and that does not confuse a vivid quarter with a durable trend. Six indicators are enough to frame the available evidence: total software revenue, cloud subscription revenue, transition in the revenue mix, gross profit and margin, operating cash flow after capital expenditures, and customer adoption evidence. The first five are drawn from reported financial statements or derived directly from them. The sixth is made up of named company-published case outcomes, which are informative examples but not audited company-wide KPIs. [1][2][6][7][8][9]

Read the six indicators as a chain. A user has to adopt the product; the customer has to renew or expand; that relationship appears in recurring revenue; revenue has to carry gross profit after service delivery; and ultimately cash has to arrive after payroll and other operating needs. A single point in that chain can look strong while the full economic loop remains weak. The supplied evidence gives you subscription revenue, gross profit, annual and interim cash flow, and selected customer-story outcomes, but it does not connect an individual cohort’s usage to renewal, margin, and collection. This is why a broad statement about product strength should be tested against several measures at once. [1][2][5][6][7][8][9]

Total software revenue was $477.233 million in FY2025 compared with $463.456 million in FY2024, a derived increase of about 3.0% using FY2024 revenue as denominator. Q3 2026 revenue was $125.427 million compared with $128.691 million in Q3 2025. You can therefore describe the annual result as modest growth and the quarterly comparison as lower, but you cannot infer bookings, pipeline, or customer expansion from recognized revenue alone. There is no multi-year customer cohort schedule in the allowed record. [1][2]

Cloud subscription revenue is the clearest positive transition signal. It rose from $106.776 million in FY2024 to $175.657 million in FY2025, a derived increase of about 64.5% based on the prior-year amount. Q3 subscription revenue was $68.590 million versus $45.972 million, about 49.2% higher by the same calculation. Growth is visible in both comparisons. What remains unreported is whether the gains came from new customer wins, converted legacy contracts, account expansion, pricing changes, or some combination, as well as whether those customers renew and at what contribution margin. [1][2]

The mix transition is not a one-line success metric. FY2025 license revenue was $39.674 million and product support was $204.225 million; for Q3 2026, licenses were $3.829 million and support $37.681 million, both below the comparable Q3 2025 values. Cloud subscriptions are rising while some legacy-associated lines are declining. The company has also set a support timetable for on-premises products, with end-of-support already begun and full support ending December 31, 2026. Without migration counts and renewal data, you cannot tell whether subscription growth is more than compensating for the decline in legacy streams across the customer base. The supplied summary does not give nine-month category detail, so do not interpolate it. [1][2]

Gross profit gives the fourth operating lens. FY2025 gross profit was $327.816 million on $477.233 million revenue. In Q3 2026, gross profit was $89.634 million on $125.427 million revenue, a derived 71.5% margin; the company release describes it as 71%. These figures show that recognized software sales carry meaningful gross profit before selling, product development, and administrative costs. They do not establish operating profitability: FY2025 gross profit was lower than the combined $368.725 million of selling and marketing, R&D, and G&A disclosed in the filing. [1][2][3]

The fifth KPI is cash generation after the modest capital expenditure line. FY2025 operating cash flow was negative $67.241 million and capex was $8.212 million. Nine-month 2026 operating cash flow was positive $14.267 million against capex of $3.181 million, versus negative $45.612 million and capex of $7.628 million in the prior-year nine-month comparison. These values imply an improvement in the interim cash picture. Management’s FY2025 statement remains a stronger warning than any one interim datapoint: the software operation did not generate positive operating cash and was not expected to produce enough to meet stated financial obligations or liquidity needs over the coming twelve months. [1][2]

The sixth indicator—customer adoption—must be labeled differently. Pfizer’s case reports utilization rising from 10% on legacy reports to 90%; Helsana says report redundancy fell by “90% plus”; Lotte reports four-times analytics usage and a 90% efficiency improvement after six months. These claims help you see the potential value of governed data, reusable templates, report rationalization, and natural-language access. They are company-reported customer examples, not a broad usage database. The company does not provide aggregate daily or monthly active users, seat utilization, retention, net expansion, satisfaction, or independent verification in the permitted evidence. [6][7][9]

Now audit management’s statements against delivery without inventing a historical promise ledger. The most explicit long-horizon goal in the allowed call excerpt is Le’s statement: “The goal is to double Bitcoin per share in seven years through the use of digital credit.” The Q3 release reports 848,517 Bitcoin held as of October 25, 26% year-to-date growth, and $14.33 billion in year-to-date purchases. These reported results show that the accumulation program was active. They do not tell you whether the per-share target is on track because the permitted evidence provides neither the baseline per-share amount nor a complete share-issuance path, and seven years have not elapsed. It is a target to monitor, not a result to credit in advance. [3][4]

Notice the difference between a delivered activity metric and a delivered outcome. A purchase amount records capital deployed and a total Bitcoin count records an aggregate balance. The stated objective is per share, so it requires an additional denominator and a way to account for financing claims and share-count changes. The source packet reports the target and total holdings but does not supply that full bridge. Until it does, the activity can be acknowledged as execution without claiming that the ultimate per-share result has already followed. [3][4]

The software evidence is directionally aligned with a cloud shift but incomplete as a walk-the-talk audit. Subscription revenue grew in FY2025 and again in the Q3 comparison, which is consistent with the stated subscription model and the phase-out of on-premises support. But total Q3 revenue and gross profit were lower year over year, while support and license revenue were also lower. The data do not include a dated management target for customer migrations, cloud revenue mix, retention, or operating cash flow. Without the target, you can describe delivery and risk but cannot fairly declare the transition achieved or missed. [1][2]

The Q3 CFO quote needs the same disciplined comparison. Kang said, “Q3 was an exceptionally strong quarter across all parts of our business. We now hold 848,517 Bitcoin and recorded a record $21 billion fair value gain on our Bitcoin holdings in Q3.” The Bitcoin count and fair-value gain are treasury facts. For software, Q3 revenue and gross profit were lower than the prior-year quarter in the supplied statements. This does not prove that every part of software weakened; it does show why a broad phrase such as “all parts” must be tested with business-specific measures rather than net income. The release’s $19.53 billion net income is substantially explained by the digital-asset mark-to-market, not by software sales. [2][3][4]

The leadership transition is another observable promise with a future test. The release says Andrew Kang would leave the CFO role effective November 5, 2026, Le would cover finance in the interim, and Reza Virasteh would become CFO in January 2027 as responsibilities were split across the software and Bitcoin activities. Le told the call, “Starting in January 2027, we will split the CFO role between our software and our Bitcoin businesses, which are quite different.” The plan could improve the clarity of accountability and reporting. The supplied materials announce it; they do not show the structure in operation or demonstrate better internal controls, capital allocation, or software cash transparency. [3][4]

The release’s treasury coverage figures also belong in their own column. It reports $1.48 billion cumulative preferred dividends paid, $5.07 billion in USD assets, and 3.4 years of dividend-plus-interest coverage as of October 25. Those company-reported figures may be relevant to the capacity of the financing model, but they are not evidence of subscription retention or software cash sufficiency. A subsequent financing review would need to trace the instruments, definitions, maturities, and obligations in detail. For this chapter, their main lesson is that a combined company needs parallel dashboards: operating KPIs for analytics and financing KPIs for treasury activity. [3]

Management’s historical follow-through cannot be scored comprehensively from this packet. The allowed sources contain a current seven-year treasury objective, a short operating history of revenue mix and cash flow, a set of vendor-published customer outcomes, and an announced finance reorganization. They do not provide a long catalogue of dated product promises and audited completion records. The honest scorecard is therefore measured rather than binary: cloud revenue expansion is delivered in the observed comparisons; the legacy migration is underway but unquantified; the customer value is illustrated but not generalized; cash flow improved in the nine-month comparison but did not erase the FY2025 warning; and the per-share treasury target and leadership design await future measurement. [1][2][3][4][6][7][8][9]

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: A fair walk-the-talk audit does not reward a target as though it were already delivered, and it does not call a directional operating signal failure because the full cohort data are missing. Credit the observed subscription growth; keep the promised per-share objective and the CFO redesign in the future tense. [1][2][3][4]

book_callouts.title: MEASUREMENT RULE
book_callouts.text: When management describes consolidated strength, split the scorecard by business. Treasury holdings and fair-value gains do not substitute for software revenue, retention, margin, or cash conversion. [2][3][4]
